{{Short description|1320s calculation of pi by Zhao Youqin}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Zhao Youqin's {{pi}} algorithm}}
[[File:Zhao Youqin circle dissection algorithm.svg|thumb|right|300px|Zhao Youqin's {{pi}} algorithm]]
[[File:赵友钦割圆术书影.JPG|thumb|300px|A page from Zhao Youqin's book ''Ge Xiang Xin Shu'' vol 5]]

'''Zhao Youqin's {{pi}} algorithm''' is an algorithm  devised by  [[Yuan dynasty]] Chinese astronomer and mathematician [[Zhao Youqin]] ({{lang|zh|赵友钦}}, ? – 1330) to calculate the value of [[Pi|{{pi}}]] in his book ''Ge Xiang Xin Shu'' ({{lang|zh|革象新书}}).

== Algorithm ==
Zhao Youqin started with an inscribed square in a circle with [[radius]] <var>r</var>.<ref>[[Yoshio Mikami]], Development of Mathematics in China and Japan, Chapter 20, The Studies about the Value of {{pi}} etc., pp&nbsp;135–138</ref>

If <math>\ell</math> denotes the length of a side of the square, draw a [[perpendicular]] line <var>d</var> from the center of the circle to side <var>l</var>. Let <var>e</var> denotes <var>r</var>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;<var>d</var>. Then from the diagram:

:<math>d=\sqrt{r^2-\left(\frac{\ell}{2}\right)^2}</math>

:<math>e=r-d=r-\sqrt{r^2-\left(\frac{\ell}{2}\right)^2}.</math>

Extend the perpendicular line <var>d</var> to dissect the circle into an [[octagon]]; <math>\ell_2</math> denotes the length of one side of octagon.

:<math>\ell_2=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\ell}{2}\right)^2+e^2}</math>

:<math>\ell_2=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ \ell^2 +4\left(r-\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{4r^2-\ell^2}\right)^2}</math>

Let  <math>l_3</math> denotes the length of a side of [[hexadecagon]]

:<math>\ell_3=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ \ell_2^2 +4\left(r-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4r^2-\ell_2^2}\right)^2    }</math>

similarly

:<math>\ell_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ \ell_n^2 +4\left(r-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4r^2-\ell_n^2}\right)^2} </math>

Proceeding in this way, he at last calculated the side of a 16384-gon, multiplying it by 16384 to obtain 3141.592 for a circle with diameter = 1000 units, or

:<math>\pi =3.141592. \,</math>

He multiplied this number by 113 and obtained {{clarify|text=355.|reason=3.141592 × 113 = 354.999896, not 355|date=March 2026}} From this he deduced that of the traditional values of {{pi}}, that is 3, 3.14, {{sfrac|22|7}} and {{sfrac|355|113}}, the last is the most exact.<ref>Yoshio Mikami, p136</ref>
